title: spark.sql() Basics – Running SQL in PySpark
description: spark.sql() allows you to execute SQL statements directly against the Spark session. It returns a DataFrame that can be further transformed or displayed. This is the entry point for all SQL-based interactions in Databricks notebooks.
code:
-- In a Databricks notebook cell (SQL mode)
-- Or via spark.sql() in PySpark:

-- 1. Simple query against an in-memory view
SELECT current_date() AS run_date, current_user() AS executed_by;

-- 2. Create a temp view from a DataFrame (PySpark interop)
-- df = spark.read.format('delta').load('/mnt/bronze/transactions')
-- df.createOrReplaceTempView('raw_transactions')

-- 3. Query the temp view via SQL
SELECT
    txn_id,
    account_id,
    txn_amount,
    txn_currency,
    txn_date
FROM raw_transactions
WHERE txn_amount > 10000
  AND txn_currency = 'EUR'
LIMIT 100;

-- 4. Set Spark SQL config within SQL
SET spark.sql.shuffle.partitions = 200;
SET spark.databricks.delta.optimizeWrite.enabled = true;

-- 5. Use spark.sql() result as DataFrame (PySpark)
-- result_df = spark.sql("""
--     SELECT account_id, SUM(txn_amount) AS total_amount
--     FROM raw_transactions
--     GROUP BY account_id
-- """)
-- result_df.display()
notes: spark.sql() returns a DataFrame — chain .display(), .show(), .write, etc.
SQL cells in Databricks use %sql magic — no need to wrap in spark.sql()
Temp views created via createOrReplaceTempView are session-scoped; Global temp views persist across sessions within the same app
SET commands configure Spark session properties and can affect query performance significantly
In Unity Catalog environments, always qualify table names: catalog.schema.table
use_case: A TCS BFSI team running ad-hoc regulatory queries on Azure Databricks — analysts write SQL while engineers orchestrate via PySpark pipelines, using spark.sql() to bridge both worlds in multi-hop Medallion Architecture notebooks.

title: Creating and Using Databases/Schemas
description: In Spark SQL, databases and schemas are synonymous terms used to logically group tables. In Unity Catalog, the hierarchy is Catalog > Schema > Table, replacing the legacy two-level Hive metastore model. Proper namespace management is foundational for any enterprise data lake.
notes: Unity Catalog uses 3-level namespace: catalog.schema.table — always use fully qualified names in production
MANAGED LOCATION specifies ADLS Gen2 path for all managed tables within the schema
USE CATALOG and USE SCHEMA set the session context — subsequent unqualified table refs resolve to these
Legacy Hive metastore uses hive_metastore as default catalog — migration to Unity Catalog is recommended
Schema-level permissions in Unity Catalog cascade to all tables within — design schemas around access boundaries
use_case: Setting up a new EU regulatory reporting workspace in Azure Databricks with Unity Catalog for a retail bank's AML (Anti-Money Laundering) compliance team — each Medallion layer gets its own schema, storage location, and access control boundary.

title: SELECT / WHERE / ORDER BY / LIMIT in Spark SQL
description: Foundational DQL (Data Query Language) operations in Spark SQL follow ANSI SQL syntax. Spark SQL supports predicate pushdown to optimize WHERE clause filtering, especially on partitioned Delta tables. ORDER BY in distributed systems is expensive — use SORT WITHIN PARTITIONS for better performance at scale.
code:
-- =============================================
-- DQL Fundamentals — EU Banking Transactions
-- =============================================

USE CATALOG eu_bfsi_prod;
USE SCHEMA silver;

-- Basic SELECT with column aliasing
SELECT
    txn_id                              AS transaction_id,
    account_id,
    UPPER(txn_type)                     AS transaction_type,
    txn_amount,
    txn_currency,
    ROUND(txn_amount * fx_rate, 2)      AS amount_in_eur,
    txn_timestamp                       AS transaction_ts,
    DATE(txn_timestamp)                 AS transaction_date
FROM silver_transactions
WHERE
    txn_date >= '2024-01-01'            -- Partition pruning benefit
    AND txn_date <  '2025-01-01'
    AND txn_currency IN ('EUR', 'GBP', 'USD')
    AND txn_amount   BETWEEN 1000 AND 1000000
    AND txn_status   != 'REVERSED'
    AND account_id   IS NOT NULL
ORDER BY txn_amount DESC
LIMIT 500;

-- DISTINCT values
SELECT DISTINCT txn_currency, txn_type
FROM silver_transactions
ORDER BY txn_currency;

-- Wildcard LIKE filter (AML keyword scan)
SELECT txn_id, merchant_name, txn_amount
FROM silver_transactions
WHERE merchant_name LIKE '%CRYPTO%'
   OR merchant_name LIKE '%OFFSHORE%'
ORDER BY txn_amount DESC;

-- NULL-safe comparisons
SELECT *
FROM silver_accounts
WHERE risk_score IS NULL
   OR credit_limit <=> 0;  -- <=> is NULL-safe equality
notes: Spark SQL supports ANSI SQL — use standard syntax; Spark-specific extensions are additive
WHERE on partition columns (e.g. txn_date) triggers partition pruning — critical for Delta table performance
ORDER BY is a full sort — it collects all data to a single partition; use only with LIMIT for large datasets
BETWEEN is inclusive on both ends: BETWEEN 1000 AND 1000000 includes both boundary values
The NULL-safe equality operator <=> returns true when both sides are NULL — unlike = which returns NULL
use_case: Compliance analysts at a European bank querying the silver transaction layer to identify high-value FX trades for regulatory EMIR reporting — partition pruning on txn_date dramatically reduces query cost on multi-billion-row Delta tables.

title: CREATE TABLE USING DELTA
description: Delta Lake is the default table format in Databricks. CREATE TABLE USING DELTA creates a versioned, ACID-compliant table backed by Parquet files and a Delta transaction log. Delta tables support schema enforcement, time travel, and DML operations unlike plain Parquet or CSV tables.
code:
-- =============================================
-- CREATE Delta Tables — EU BFSI Bronze Layer
-- =============================================

USE CATALOG eu_bfsi_prod;
USE SCHEMA bronze;

-- Managed Delta table (storage managed by Unity Catalog)
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS bronze_transactions (
    txn_id          STRING          NOT NULL COMMENT 'Unique transaction identifier from source',
    account_id      STRING          NOT NULL COMMENT 'Source account identifier',
    counterparty_id STRING                   COMMENT 'Beneficiary account or counterparty',
    txn_amount      DECIMAL(18, 4)  NOT NULL COMMENT 'Transaction amount in originating currency',
    txn_currency    STRING(3)       NOT NULL COMMENT 'ISO 4217 currency code',
    txn_type        STRING                   COMMENT 'CREDIT, DEBIT, FEE, REVERSAL',
    txn_status      STRING                   COMMENT 'PENDING, COMPLETED, REVERSED, FAILED',
    txn_timestamp   TIMESTAMP       NOT NULL COMMENT 'Transaction initiation timestamp (UTC)',
    value_date      DATE                     COMMENT 'Settlement date',
    source_system   STRING                   COMMENT 'Origin system: CORE_BANKING, SWIFT, SEPA',
    ingestion_ts    TIMESTAMP       NOT NULL COMMENT 'Databricks ingestion timestamp',
    batch_id        STRING                   COMMENT 'Pipeline run batch identifier',
    _rescued_data   STRING                   COMMENT 'Auto Loader rescued data column'
)
USING DELTA
PARTITIONED BY (txn_date DATE GENERATED ALWAYS AS (DATE(txn_timestamp)))
CLUSTER BY (account_id, txn_currency)       -- Liquid clustering (post-DBR 13.3)
COMMENT 'Raw transaction events ingested from Core Banking and SWIFT — Bronze layer'
TBLPROPERTIES (
    'delta.enableChangeDataFeed'            = 'true',
    'delta.autoOptimize.optimizeWrite'      = 'true',
    'delta.autoOptimize.autoCompact'        = 'true',
    'delta.columnMapping.mode'              = 'name',
    'delta.minReaderVersion'                = '2',
    'delta.minWriterVersion'                = '5',
    'pipelines.autoOptimize.zOrderCols'     = 'account_id',
    'quality.layer'                         = 'bronze',
    'data.owner'                            = 'data-engineering@bank.eu',
    'data.classification'                   = 'CONFIDENTIAL'
);

-- External Delta table (unmanaged — storage controlled externally)
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS bronze_swift_messages
USING DELTA
LOCATION 'abfss://bronze@euadlsprod.dfs.core.windows.net/swift/messages/'
COMMENT 'SWIFT MT messages — external Delta table';
notes: USING DELTA is the default in Databricks — explicitly stating it is good practice for documentation clarity
PARTITIONED BY on a GENERATED ALWAYS AS column avoids user error while enforcing partition consistency
CLUSTER BY (Liquid Clustering) is the modern replacement for static partitioning — more flexible re-clustering without full rewrites
TBLPROPERTIES stores metadata and enables features like CDF, column mapping, and auto-optimize
Managed tables: Unity Catalog controls storage. External tables: you control storage but UC manages metadata
use_case: A data engineering team at a European custodian bank creating the bronze layer for SWIFT and Core Banking ingestion — Delta's ACID guarantees mean concurrent Auto Loader streams can ingest safely without corrupting the table.

title: INSERT INTO and INSERT OVERWRITE
description: INSERT INTO appends records to a Delta table atomically. INSERT OVERWRITE replaces table (or partition) data in a single atomic operation, making it ideal for idempotent batch loads. Delta's transaction log ensures both operations are ACID-compliant and recoverable.
code:
-- =============================================
-- INSERT Operations on Delta Tables
-- EU BFSI — Loading Reference Data
-- =============================================

USE CATALOG eu_bfsi_prod;
USE SCHEMA bronze;

-- 1. INSERT INTO — Append rows
INSERT INTO bronze_transactions
SELECT
    txn_id,
    account_id,
    counterparty_id,
    CAST(txn_amount AS DECIMAL(18,4)),
    txn_currency,
    txn_type,
    txn_status,
    CAST(txn_timestamp AS TIMESTAMP),
    CAST(value_date AS DATE),
    source_system,
    current_timestamp()                 AS ingestion_ts,
    '${batch_id}'                       AS batch_id,
    NULL                                AS _rescued_data
FROM bronze_transactions_staging
WHERE batch_id = '${batch_id}';

-- 2. INSERT OVERWRITE — Replace partition atomically
INSERT OVERWRITE eu_bfsi_prod.silver.silver_fx_rates
PARTITION (rate_date = '2024-12-31')
SELECT
    base_currency,
    target_currency,
    exchange_rate,
    source,
    current_timestamp() AS loaded_ts
FROM eu_bfsi_prod.bronze.bronze_fx_rates
WHERE rate_date = '2024-12-31'
  AND source = 'ECB';

-- 3. INSERT with VALUES (small reference loads)
INSERT INTO eu_bfsi_prod.silver.dim_currency
    (currency_code, currency_name, is_eu_currency, created_ts)
VALUES
    ('EUR', 'Euro',           true,  current_timestamp()),
    ('GBP', 'British Pound',  false, current_timestamp()),
    ('CHF', 'Swiss Franc',    false, current_timestamp()),
    ('DKK', 'Danish Krone',   false, current_timestamp()),
    ('SEK', 'Swedish Krona',  false, current_timestamp());

-- 4. INSERT OVERWRITE (full table replace — idempotent)
INSERT OVERWRITE eu_bfsi_prod.gold.gold_country_risk
SELECT country_code, risk_tier, updated_date
FROM eu_bfsi_prod.silver.silver_country_risk_staging;
notes: INSERT INTO is idempotent only with deduplication logic — without it, rerunning adds duplicates
INSERT OVERWRITE on Delta replaces entire table or specific partition atomically — safe for reruns
Delta's transaction log records every INSERT as a new version — enabling time travel rollback
Use INSERT OVERWRITE for daily/monthly partition refreshes; MERGE INTO for upsert patterns
Schema validation is enforced on INSERT — column types must match or be castable to target schema
use_case: Daily ECB FX rate refresh for a European investment bank — INSERT OVERWRITE on the rate_date partition ensures idempotent pipeline runs without risk of duplicate exchange rates corrupting downstream P&L calculations.

title: DESCRIBE TABLE / DESCRIBE EXTENDED / SHOW TABLES
description: DESCRIBE and SHOW commands are essential for understanding table schemas, metadata, storage locations, and table properties without opening external tools. In Unity Catalog environments, these commands expose catalog-level metadata including owner, creation time, and data classification tags.
notes: DESCRIBE EXTENDED is the go-to for debugging table issues — reveals location, format, owner, and properties
DESCRIBE HISTORY is unique to Delta Lake — shows full audit trail of all DML/DDL operations with timestamps
SHOW CREATE TABLE is invaluable for documentation and reproducing table DDL in new environments
SHOW TBLPROPERTIES helps verify Delta features like CDF, column mapping, and optimize settings
In Unity Catalog, DESCRIBE TABLE EXTENDED shows the securable object's owner and creation metadata
use_case: A data governance team at a European insurance company auditing table ownership and storage locations before migrating from Hive Metastore to Unity Catalog — DESCRIBE EXTENDED and SHOW CREATE TABLE help automate the migration DDL generation.

title: Basic SQL Functions: CAST, COALESCE, NVL, ISNULL
description: Type conversion and null-handling functions are the building blocks of data quality transformations in the silver layer. CAST enforces type safety, while COALESCE/NVL/ISNULL provide null-handling patterns that prevent downstream aggregation errors in financial reporting.
code:
-- =============================================
-- Type Conversion & NULL Handling
-- EU BFSI Silver Layer Data Cleansing
-- =============================================

USE CATALOG eu_bfsi_prod;
USE SCHEMA silver;

SELECT
    -- CAST: Explicit type conversion
    txn_id,
    CAST(txn_amount AS DECIMAL(18, 4))              AS txn_amount_decimal,
    CAST(txn_timestamp AS DATE)                     AS txn_date,
    CAST(txn_timestamp AS STRING)                   AS txn_ts_str,
    CAST('2024-12-31' AS DATE)                      AS end_date,
    CAST(is_international AS BOOLEAN)               AS international_flag,

    -- COALESCE: Returns first non-null value
    COALESCE(merchant_name, counterparty_name,
             beneficiary_name, 'UNKNOWN')           AS resolved_party_name,
    COALESCE(fx_rate, 1.0)                          AS fx_rate_with_default,
    COALESCE(credit_limit, overdraft_limit, 0.0)    AS effective_limit,

    -- NVL: Identical to COALESCE(expr, default) — Hive/Spark compatibility
    NVL(risk_score, 0)                              AS risk_score_safe,
    NVL(branch_code, 'ONLINE')                      AS branch_code_safe,

    -- ISNULL / ISNOTNULL / IFNULL
    ISNULL(reversal_reference)                      AS is_reversal,
    ISNOTNULL(settlement_date)                      AS is_settled,
    IFNULL(processing_fee, 0.00)                    AS processing_fee_safe,

    -- NVL2: NVL2(expr, if_not_null, if_null)
    NVL2(counterparty_country, 
         CONCAT('CROSS-BORDER:', counterparty_country), 
         'DOMESTIC')                                AS txn_geography,

    -- Combining CAST + COALESCE for safe numeric operations
    CAST(COALESCE(txn_amount, 0) AS DECIMAL(18,4))
        * CAST(COALESCE(fx_rate, 1.0) AS DECIMAL(10,6))  AS amount_eur,

    -- NULLIF: Returns NULL if two values are equal
    NULLIF(error_code, '')                          AS error_code_clean,  -- Empty string to NULL
    NULLIF(txn_count, 0)                            AS txn_count_nonzero  -- 0 to NULL (safe division)

FROM bronze_transactions
WHERE ingestion_date = current_date();
notes: COALESCE is ANSI SQL and evaluates arguments left to right — use it over NVL for portability
NULLIF(value, '') is the idiomatic way to convert empty strings to NULL in cleansing pipelines
CAST is strict — use TRY_CAST to return NULL instead of throwing on invalid conversions
DECIMAL(18,4) is the recommended type for financial amounts — avoids floating-point precision errors
NVL is Hive-compatible syntax supported in Spark SQL; prefer COALESCE in new code for ANSI compliance
use_case: Silver layer data cleansing pipeline at a European payments processor — raw Core Banking data arrives with mixed types and nulls; CAST and COALESCE transforms ensure downstream gold layer aggregations produce accurate SEPA reporting figures.

title: Reading Files Directly with SQL (CSV, JSON, Parquet)
description: Spark SQL supports querying files directly without defining a table, using the `format.\`path\`` syntax. This is useful for data exploration, one-time loads, and Auto Loader alternative ingestion. Delta, Parquet, JSON, CSV, and Avro are all supported inline in SELECT statements.
code:
-- =============================================
-- Direct File Querying in Spark SQL
-- EU BFSI — Exploring Raw Ingestion Files
-- =============================================

-- 1. Read CSV directly (with inferred schema)
SELECT *
FROM csv.`abfss://raw@euadlsprod.dfs.core.windows.net/ecb_fx_rates/2024/12/31/`
LIMIT 100;

-- 2. Read CSV with explicit schema and options
SELECT *
FROM read_files(
    'abfss://raw@euadlsprod.dfs.core.windows.net/ecb_fx_rates/2024/',
    format => 'csv',
    header => 'true',
    inferSchema => 'true',
    sep => ','
);

-- 3. Read Parquet file/directory
SELECT
    account_id,
    balance,
    as_of_date
FROM parquet.`abfss://bronze@euadlsprod.dfs.core.windows.net/account_balances/year=2024/month=12/`
WHERE as_of_date >= '2024-12-01';

-- 4. Read JSON (SWIFT MT103 messages)
SELECT
    get_json_object(value, '$.MessageType')     AS msg_type,
    get_json_object(value, '$.TransactionRef')  AS txn_ref,
    get_json_object(value, '$.Amount.Value')    AS amount,
    get_json_object(value, '$.Amount.Currency') AS currency,
    get_json_object(value, '$.ValueDate')       AS value_date
FROM json.`abfss://raw@euadlsprod.dfs.core.windows.net/swift/mt103/2024/12/`
LIMIT 200;

-- 5. Read Delta files directly
SELECT * FROM delta.`abfss://bronze@euadlsprod.dfs.core.windows.net/transactions/`
LIMIT 50;

-- 6. Create a table from file (CTAS)
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS eu_bfsi_prod.bronze.bronze_ecb_fx
USING DELTA
AS
SELECT
    _metadata.file_path          AS source_file,
    _metadata.file_modification_time AS file_ts,
    *
FROM read_files(
    'abfss://raw@euadlsprod.dfs.core.windows.net/ecb_fx_rates/',
    format => 'csv',
    header => 'true',
    inferSchema => 'true'
);
notes: format.`path` syntax works for delta, parquet, json, csv, avro, orc — convenient for exploration
read_files() is the modern Databricks SQL function with richer options including schema hints
_metadata columns (file_path, file_size, file_modification_time) are auto-populated by Spark for traceability
Direct file queries don't benefit from Delta optimizations — create a Delta table for production use
CTAS (CREATE TABLE AS SELECT) is the fastest way to materialize exploratory queries into Delta tables
use_case: A data engineer at a European asset manager exploring newly landed ECB exchange rate CSV files in ADLS Gen2 before defining the formal bronze table schema — direct SQL querying saves time compared to writing full PySpark read/display code.

title: CTEs (Common Table Expressions) in Spark SQL
description: CTEs (WITH clauses) improve query readability and maintainability by naming intermediate result sets. Spark SQL supports multiple CTEs in a single WITH block and recursive CTEs. In BFSI pipelines, CTEs help decompose complex multi-step transformations into readable, testable units.
code:
-- =============================================
-- CTEs for Complex BFSI Analytics
-- AML Transaction Monitoring Pipeline
-- =============================================

USE CATALOG eu_bfsi_prod;
USE SCHEMA gold;

WITH
-- CTE 1: Base transaction data with FX normalization
normalized_txns AS (
    SELECT
        t.txn_id,
        t.account_id,
        t.txn_amount,
        t.txn_currency,
        t.txn_amount * COALESCE(fx.exchange_rate, 1.0)  AS amount_eur,
        t.txn_type,
        t.txn_timestamp,
        DATE(t.txn_timestamp)                            AS txn_date,
        t.counterparty_country,
        t.source_system
    FROM eu_bfsi_prod.silver.silver_transactions t
    LEFT JOIN eu_bfsi_prod.silver.silver_fx_rates fx
        ON t.txn_currency = fx.from_currency
        AND DATE(t.txn_timestamp) = fx.rate_date
        AND fx.to_currency = 'EUR'
    WHERE t.txn_date BETWEEN '2024-01-01' AND '2024-12-31'
      AND t.txn_status = 'COMPLETED'
),

-- CTE 2: Daily account aggregates
daily_account_aggregates AS (
    SELECT
        account_id,
        txn_date,
        COUNT(*)                    AS txn_count,
        SUM(amount_eur)             AS daily_debit_eur,
        MAX(amount_eur)             AS max_single_txn_eur,
        COUNT(DISTINCT counterparty_country) AS unique_countries
    FROM normalized_txns
    WHERE txn_type = 'DEBIT'
    GROUP BY account_id, txn_date
),

-- CTE 3: Accounts with high-risk patterns
high_risk_accounts AS (
    SELECT
        account_id,
        AVG(daily_debit_eur)        AS avg_daily_debit,
        MAX(daily_debit_eur)        AS peak_daily_debit,
        SUM(txn_count)              AS total_txns,
        MAX(unique_countries)       AS max_countries_in_day
    FROM daily_account_aggregates
    GROUP BY account_id
    HAVING  AVG(daily_debit_eur) > 50000
        OR  MAX(unique_countries) >= 5
        OR  MAX(daily_debit_eur)  > 250000
),

-- CTE 4: Account profile enrichment
account_profile AS (
    SELECT
        a.account_id,
        a.customer_id,
        a.account_type,
        a.risk_tier,
        c.customer_name,
        c.nationality,
        c.pep_flag,         -- Politically Exposed Person
        c.sanction_flag
    FROM eu_bfsi_prod.silver.silver_accounts a
    JOIN eu_bfsi_prod.silver.silver_customers c
        ON a.customer_id = c.customer_id
)

-- Final output: AML alert candidates
SELECT
    hr.account_id,
    ap.customer_name,
    ap.nationality,
    ap.pep_flag,
    ap.sanction_flag,
    ap.risk_tier,
    hr.avg_daily_debit,
    hr.peak_daily_debit,
    hr.total_txns,
    hr.max_countries_in_day,
    CASE
        WHEN ap.sanction_flag = true         THEN 'CRITICAL'
        WHEN ap.pep_flag = true              THEN 'HIGH'
        WHEN hr.peak_daily_debit > 500000   THEN 'HIGH'
        WHEN hr.max_countries_in_day >= 10  THEN 'MEDIUM'
        ELSE                                     'LOW'
    END                                     AS alert_priority,
    current_timestamp()                     AS alert_generated_ts
FROM high_risk_accounts hr
JOIN account_profile ap ON hr.account_id = ap.account_id
ORDER BY alert_priority, hr.peak_daily_debit DESC;
notes: CTEs are not materialized by default in Spark — they are inlined into the query plan; use temp views for reuse across multiple queries
Multiple CTEs in one WITH block are separated by commas — later CTEs can reference earlier ones
CTEs vastly improve query readability vs deeply nested subqueries — prefer them in code reviews
For expensive intermediate results reused multiple times, consider CACHE TABLE or a temp view materialization
Spark SQL supports recursive CTEs (WITH RECURSIVE) since Spark 3.4 — useful for hierarchy traversal
use_case: AML transaction monitoring pipeline at a pan-European retail bank — CTEs decompose the complex multi-join, multi-aggregation alert generation query into readable stages that can be individually unit-tested and reviewed by compliance teams.

title: Window Functions in Spark SQL
description: Window functions perform calculations across a set of rows related to the current row without collapsing the result set. Essential for running totals, rankings, lag/lead comparisons, and period-over-period analytics in financial reporting. Spark SQL implements the full ANSI SQL window function standard.
code:
-- =============================================
-- Window Functions — EU Banking Analytics
-- Account Balance & Transaction Trend Analysis
-- =============================================

USE CATALOG eu_bfsi_prod;
USE SCHEMA gold;

SELECT
    account_id,
    txn_date,
    txn_id,
    txn_amount,
    txn_type,

    -- RANKING functions
    ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
        PARTITION BY account_id
        ORDER BY txn_timestamp DESC
    )                                               AS txn_recency_rank,

    RANK() OVER (
        PARTITION BY account_id, MONTH(txn_date)
        ORDER BY txn_amount DESC
    )                                               AS monthly_amount_rank,

    DENSE_RANK() OVER (
        PARTITION BY account_id
        ORDER BY DATE(txn_date)
    )                                               AS day_sequence,

    -- VALUE functions: LAG / LEAD
    LAG(txn_amount, 1, 0) OVER (
        PARTITION BY account_id
        ORDER BY txn_timestamp
    )                                               AS prev_txn_amount,

    txn_amount - LAG(txn_amount, 1, 0) OVER (
        PARTITION BY account_id
        ORDER BY txn_timestamp
    )                                               AS amount_delta_from_prev,

    LEAD(txn_date, 1) OVER (
        PARTITION BY account_id
        ORDER BY txn_timestamp
    )                                               AS next_txn_date,

    -- AGGREGATE window functions
    SUM(txn_amount) OVER (
        PARTITION BY account_id
        ORDER BY txn_timestamp
        ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
    )                                               AS running_total,

    AVG(txn_amount) OVER (
        PARTITION BY account_id
        ORDER BY txn_date
        ROWS BETWEEN 6 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW
    )                                               AS rolling_7day_avg,

    SUM(txn_amount) OVER (
        PARTITION BY account_id, YEAR(txn_date), MONTH(txn_date)
    )                                               AS monthly_total,

    -- FIRST_VALUE / LAST_VALUE
    FIRST_VALUE(txn_amount) OVER (
        PARTITION BY account_id, DATE(txn_date)
        ORDER BY txn_timestamp
        ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING
    )                                               AS first_txn_of_day,

    LAST_VALUE(txn_amount) OVER (
        PARTITION BY account_id, DATE(txn_date)
        ORDER BY txn_timestamp
        ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING
    )                                               AS last_txn_of_day,

    -- NTILE: Quartile bucketing
    NTILE(4) OVER (
        PARTITION BY YEAR(txn_date)
        ORDER BY txn_amount
    )                                               AS amount_quartile,

    -- PERCENT_RANK / CUME_DIST
    ROUND(PERCENT_RANK() OVER (
        PARTITION BY account_id
        ORDER BY txn_amount
    ), 4)                                           AS pct_rank_in_account,

    ROUND(CUME_DIST() OVER (
        ORDER BY txn_amount
    ), 4)                                           AS cumulative_distribution

FROM eu_bfsi_prod.silver.silver_transactions
WHERE txn_date BETWEEN '2024-01-01' AND '2024-12-31'
  AND txn_status = 'COMPLETED'
  AND txn_type = 'DEBIT'
QUALIFY txn_recency_rank <= 10;  -- Databricks-specific: filter on window result
notes: PARTITION BY is optional — omitting it makes the window span the entire dataset (use carefully on large tables)
ROWS BETWEEN vs RANGE BETWEEN: ROWS is physical (N rows before/after), RANGE is logical (based on ORDER BY value)
QUALIFY clause (Databricks extension) filters on window function results without a subquery wrapper
LAG/LEAD default value (3rd parameter) prevents NULL in first/last rows — always provide defaults for financial calcs
Window functions are computed after WHERE/GROUP BY/HAVING but before ORDER BY and LIMIT
use_case: A European investment bank's risk analytics team calculating rolling 7-day average transaction amounts and running totals per account to detect structuring patterns (breaking large transactions into smaller ones to evade AML thresholds) — window functions make this a single-pass SQL query.

title: Complex Types: Arrays, Maps, Structs — EXPLODE, COLLECT_LIST
description: Spark SQL's support for nested data types (ARRAY, MAP, STRUCT) enables working with semi-structured data natively without denormalization. EXPLODE converts arrays/maps into rows, while COLLECT_LIST/COLLECT_SET aggregate rows back into arrays. Critical for processing JSON-based financial messages.
code:
-- =============================================
-- Complex Types in Spark SQL
-- EU BFSI — SWIFT & Trade Finance Messages
-- =============================================

USE CATALOG eu_bfsi_prod;
USE SCHEMA silver;

-- 1. Querying STRUCT fields (dot notation)
SELECT
    txn_id,
    counterparty.bank_name                  AS cp_bank,
    counterparty.bic_code                   AS cp_bic,
    counterparty.country                    AS cp_country,
    amount_details.value                    AS txn_value,
    amount_details.currency                 AS txn_currency,
    amount_details.fx_rate                  AS applied_rate
FROM silver_swift_mt103
WHERE counterparty.country NOT IN ('GB', 'US', 'EU')
  AND amount_details.value > 100000;

-- 2. EXPLODE array — one row per array element
SELECT
    trade_id,
    leg_idx,               -- Position in original array
    leg.leg_type           AS leg_type,
    leg.notional           AS leg_notional,
    leg.currency           AS leg_currency,
    leg.maturity_date      AS leg_maturity
FROM silver_trade_legs
LATERAL VIEW POSEXPLODE(trade_legs) AS leg_idx, leg
WHERE leg.leg_type IN ('FIXED', 'FLOATING');

-- 3. EXPLODE map — one row per key-value pair
SELECT
    account_id,
    attr_key,
    attr_value
FROM silver_account_attributes
LATERAL VIEW EXPLODE(attribute_map) AS attr_key, attr_value
WHERE attr_key IN ('RISK_TIER', 'KYC_STATUS', 'PRODUCT_CODE');

-- 4. COLLECT_LIST — aggregate rows into array
SELECT
    account_id,
    COLLECT_LIST(txn_id)                    AS all_txn_ids,
    COLLECT_LIST(
        STRUCT(txn_id, txn_amount, txn_date)
    )                                       AS txn_details,
    SIZE(COLLECT_LIST(txn_id))              AS txn_count,
    COLLECT_SET(txn_currency)               AS unique_currencies,
    ARRAY_SORT(COLLECT_SET(counterparty_country)) AS countries_dealt_with
FROM silver_transactions
WHERE txn_date >= '2024-01-01'
GROUP BY account_id;

-- 5. Array manipulation functions
SELECT
    account_id,
    flagged_txn_ids,
    ARRAY_CONTAINS(flagged_txn_ids, '${alert_txn_id}')   AS in_alert_list,
    ARRAY_SIZE(flagged_txn_ids)                           AS flag_count,
    FILTER(flagged_txn_ids, x -> x LIKE 'TXN-EU%')       AS eu_flagged_only,
    TRANSFORM(txn_amounts, x -> x * 1.20)                AS amounts_with_vat,
    AGGREGATE(txn_amounts, 0D, (acc, x) -> acc + x)      AS total_amount,
    FLATTEN(ARRAY(txn_ids_q1, txn_ids_q2, txn_ids_q3, txn_ids_q4)) AS all_year_txns
FROM silver_account_summary;

-- 6. Struct construction and from_json
SELECT
    txn_id,
    STRUCT(
        account_id      AS account,
        txn_amount      AS amount,
        txn_currency    AS currency
    )                                       AS txn_core_struct,
    FROM_JSON(
        raw_payload,
        'STRUCT<sender_bic:STRING, receiver_bic:STRING, ref:STRING>'
    )                                       AS parsed_payload
FROM bronze_transactions;
notes: POSEXPLODE returns both the index and the element — use it when array position matters (e.g., trade legs order)
COLLECT_LIST preserves duplicates; COLLECT_SET removes them — choose based on whether deduplication is needed
FILTER, TRANSFORM, AGGREGATE are higher-order functions that accept lambda expressions — powerful for array operations
from_json/to_json enable parsing JSON strings into typed structs without exploding to rows
Struct columns support dot notation for field access — nested structs can be chained: col.nested.field
use_case: Processing SWIFT MT103 and ISO 20022 trade finance messages at a European correspondent bank — JSON payloads with nested arrays of trade legs and MAP-typed attribute collections are parsed and exploded in the silver layer transformation pipeline.

title: JOIN Types in Spark SQL
description: Spark SQL supports all standard SQL JOIN types plus Spark-specific extensions. Understanding join strategies (broadcast, shuffle hash, sort merge) is critical for performance in large-scale BFSI joins between fact and dimension tables. The USING clause simplifies equi-joins on identically named columns.
code:
-- =============================================
-- JOIN Patterns in EU BFSI Analytics
-- Transaction Enrichment Pipeline
-- =============================================

USE CATALOG eu_bfsi_prod;
USE SCHEMA gold;

-- 1. INNER JOIN — most common, only matching rows
SELECT
    t.txn_id,
    t.account_id,
    t.txn_amount,
    a.account_type,
    a.risk_tier,
    c.customer_name
FROM silver_transactions t
INNER JOIN silver_accounts a ON t.account_id = a.account_id
INNER JOIN silver_customers c ON a.customer_id = c.customer_id
WHERE t.txn_date = current_date();

-- 2. LEFT JOIN — keep all transactions, enrich where possible
SELECT
    t.txn_id,
    t.txn_amount,
    t.txn_currency,
    COALESCE(fx.exchange_rate, 1.0)     AS fx_rate,
    t.txn_amount * COALESCE(fx.exchange_rate, 1.0) AS amount_eur
FROM silver_transactions t
LEFT JOIN silver_fx_rates fx
    ON t.txn_currency = fx.from_currency
    AND DATE(t.txn_timestamp) = fx.rate_date
    AND fx.to_currency = 'EUR';

-- 3. ANTI JOIN — find unmatched records (data quality)
SELECT t.txn_id, t.account_id, t.txn_amount
FROM bronze_transactions t
LEFT ANTI JOIN silver_transactions s ON t.txn_id = s.txn_id
WHERE t.ingestion_date = current_date();
-- Finds bronze records not yet promoted to silver

-- 4. SEMI JOIN — filter on existence (no columns from right side)
SELECT account_id, customer_id, risk_tier
FROM silver_accounts
WHERE account_id IN (
    SELECT DISTINCT account_id
    FROM silver_transactions
    WHERE txn_amount > 1000000
      AND txn_date >= '2024-01-01'
);
-- Equivalent SEMI JOIN syntax:
SELECT a.account_id, a.customer_id, a.risk_tier
FROM silver_accounts a
LEFT SEMI JOIN silver_transactions t
    ON a.account_id = t.account_id
    AND t.txn_amount > 1000000
    AND t.txn_date >= '2024-01-01';

-- 5. CROSS JOIN — use with extreme caution (Cartesian product)
SELECT
    c.currency_code,
    r.region_code,
    CONCAT(c.currency_code, '_', r.region_code) AS segment_key
FROM dim_currency c
CROSS JOIN dim_region r;  -- Safe only on small dimension tables

-- 6. USING clause — same-named column equi-join
SELECT t.txn_id, t.txn_amount, a.account_type
FROM silver_transactions t
JOIN silver_accounts a USING (account_id);

-- 7. NON-EQUI JOIN — join with range condition
SELECT
    t.txn_id,
    t.txn_amount,
    r.risk_category
FROM silver_transactions t
JOIN dim_amount_risk_bands r
    ON t.txn_amount BETWEEN r.min_amount AND r.max_amount
    AND t.txn_currency = r.currency;

-- 8. FULL OUTER JOIN — reconciliation pattern
SELECT
    COALESCE(s.txn_id, t.txn_id)           AS txn_id,
    s.txn_amount                            AS source_amount,
    t.txn_amount                            AS target_amount,
    s.txn_amount - t.txn_amount             AS variance,
    CASE
        WHEN s.txn_id IS NULL THEN 'TARGET_ONLY'
        WHEN t.txn_id IS NULL THEN 'SOURCE_ONLY'
        ELSE 'MATCHED'
    END                                     AS reconciliation_status
FROM silver_source_transactions s
FULL OUTER JOIN silver_target_transactions t ON s.txn_id = t.txn_id;
notes: ANTI JOIN and SEMI JOIN are Spark SQL extensions — they're highly efficient because the right table is only used for filtering
Broadcast join is automatically chosen when one side is small (<= spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold, default 10MB)
FULL OUTER JOIN is the reconciliation pattern — ideal for source-to-target data quality checks
Non-equi joins (BETWEEN, >, <) cannot use hash join — Spark falls back to sort-merge join, which can be expensive
The USING clause automatically deduplicates the join column in the output — the ON clause keeps both sides
use_case: Transaction enrichment pipeline in a European bank's silver layer — LEFT JOINs add FX rates and account details while ANTI JOINs identify bronze records that failed silver promotion, enabling automated re-processing alerts in the monitoring dashboard.

title: GROUP BY Extensions: ROLLUP, CUBE, GROUPING SETS
description: ROLLUP, CUBE, and GROUPING SETS are SQL extensions that generate multiple levels of aggregation in a single query pass. Essential for financial reporting where subtotals, grand totals, and cross-dimensional summaries are needed simultaneously — replacing multiple UNION ALL queries with a single, efficient operation.
code:
-- =============================================
-- GROUP BY Extensions — EU BFSI Regulatory Reporting
-- EBA COREP / FINREP Multi-dimensional Aggregation
-- =============================================

USE CATALOG eu_bfsi_prod;
USE SCHEMA gold;

-- 1. ROLLUP — hierarchical subtotals (right-to-left)
-- Produces: (region, country, currency), (region, country), (region), ()
SELECT
    COALESCE(region, 'ALL_REGIONS')         AS region,
    COALESCE(country_code, 'ALL_COUNTRIES') AS country_code,
    COALESCE(txn_currency, 'ALL_CURRENCIES') AS txn_currency,
    SUM(txn_amount_eur)                     AS total_amount_eur,
    COUNT(DISTINCT txn_id)                  AS txn_count,
    COUNT(DISTINCT account_id)              AS unique_accounts,
    GROUPING(region)                        AS is_region_subtotal,
    GROUPING(country_code)                  AS is_country_subtotal,
    GROUPING(txn_currency)                  AS is_currency_subtotal,
    GROUPING_ID(region, country_code, txn_currency) AS grouping_level
FROM gold_txn_summary
WHERE report_period = '2024-Q4'
GROUP BY ROLLUP(region, country_code, txn_currency)
ORDER BY grouping_level DESC, region, country_code, txn_currency;

-- 2. CUBE — all combinations of GROUP BY columns
-- Produces every combination: 2^N grouping sets for N columns
SELECT
    COALESCE(txn_type, 'ALL')               AS txn_type,
    COALESCE(risk_tier, 'ALL')              AS risk_tier,
    COALESCE(product_code, 'ALL')           AS product_code,
    SUM(txn_amount_eur)                     AS total_eur,
    AVG(txn_amount_eur)                     AS avg_eur,
    COUNT(*)                                AS txn_count
FROM gold_txn_summary
GROUP BY CUBE(txn_type, risk_tier, product_code)
HAVING SUM(txn_amount_eur) > 1000000
ORDER BY GROUPING_ID(txn_type, risk_tier, product_code) DESC;

-- 3. GROUPING SETS — explicit control over which combinations
-- For FINREP: need (country), (product), (country, product), and grand total
SELECT
    country_code,
    product_code,
    txn_currency,
    SUM(exposure_amount_eur)                AS total_exposure,
    COUNT(DISTINCT counterparty_id)         AS counterparty_count,
    GROUPING_ID(country_code, product_code, txn_currency) AS grp_id
FROM gold_regulatory_exposure
WHERE reporting_date = '2024-12-31'
GROUP BY GROUPING SETS (
    (country_code),
    (product_code),
    (txn_currency),
    (country_code, product_code),
    (country_code, txn_currency),
    ()  -- Grand total row
)
ORDER BY grp_id DESC, total_exposure DESC;
notes: GROUPING() returns 1 if column is aggregated (subtotal row), 0 if it's a detail row — use with COALESCE for labeling
GROUPING_ID() returns a bit-mask integer identifying which columns are aggregated — useful for downstream filtering
ROLLUP(a, b, c) is equivalent to GROUPING SETS ((a,b,c),(a,b),(a),()) — N+1 sets for N columns
CUBE(a,b,c) generates 2^N grouping sets — use GROUPING SETS for explicit control to avoid unnecessary computation
These extensions are critical for single-pass generation of regulatory reports (COREP, FINREP, EMIR) at multiple hierarchy levels
use_case: Generating EBA FINREP regulatory exposure reports for a pan-European bank — GROUPING SETS produces country-level, product-level, and grand-total summaries in a single optimized query, replacing the 5 separate UNION ALL queries that previously caused the daily reporting job to exceed the SLA window.

title: PIVOT and UNPIVOT in Spark SQL
description: PIVOT rotates rows into columns, transforming long-format data into wide-format reports. UNPIVOT is the reverse operation. These are essential for financial matrix reports, period-over-period comparisons, and cross-tabulation reporting required by regulatory bodies.
code:
-- =============================================
-- PIVOT / UNPIVOT — EU BFSI Reporting
-- Monthly P&L and Exposure Matrix Reports
-- =============================================

USE CATALOG eu_bfsi_prod;
USE SCHEMA gold;

-- 1. PIVOT: Monthly transaction volumes by product type
SELECT *
FROM (
    SELECT
        account_id,
        DATE_FORMAT(txn_date, 'MMM-yyyy')   AS txn_month,
        product_code,
        txn_amount_eur
    FROM gold_txn_summary
    WHERE txn_date BETWEEN '2024-01-01' AND '2024-12-31'
)
PIVOT (
    ROUND(SUM(txn_amount_eur) / 1000000, 2) AS vol_meur  -- Millions EUR
    FOR product_code IN (
        'MORTGAGE'  AS mortgage,
        'PERSONAL'  AS personal_loan,
        'CURRENT'   AS current_acct,
        'SAVINGS'   AS savings_acct,
        'TRADE_FIN' AS trade_finance,
        'FX_SPOT'   AS fx_spot
    )
);
-- Output columns: account_id, txn_month, mortgage, personal_loan, ...

-- 2. PIVOT with multiple aggregations per column
SELECT *
FROM (
    SELECT country_code, risk_tier, txn_amount_eur
    FROM gold_regulatory_exposure
    WHERE reporting_date = '2024-12-31'
)
PIVOT (
    ROUND(SUM(txn_amount_eur)/1e9, 2)   AS sum_geur,
    COUNT(*)                            AS cnt
    FOR risk_tier IN ('LOW' AS low, 'MEDIUM' AS med, 'HIGH' AS high, 'CRITICAL' AS crit)
);
-- Output: country_code, low_sum_geur, low_cnt, med_sum_geur, med_cnt, ...

-- 3. Dynamic PIVOT (using Spark SQL + Python wrapper)
-- Note: Spark SQL PIVOT requires static column list
-- For dynamic pivoting, generate SQL in PySpark:
/*
pivot_cols = spark.sql("""
    SELECT DISTINCT risk_tier FROM gold_regulatory_exposure
    WHERE reporting_date = '2024-12-31'
    ORDER BY risk_tier
""").rdd.flatMap(lambda x: x).collect()

pivot_expr = ', '.join([f"'{col}' AS {col.lower().replace(' ','_')}" for col in pivot_cols])
dynamic_pivot_sql = f"""
    SELECT * FROM (
        SELECT country_code, risk_tier, txn_amount_eur
        FROM gold_regulatory_exposure WHERE reporting_date = '2024-12-31'
    ) PIVOT (SUM(txn_amount_eur) FOR risk_tier IN ({pivot_expr}))
"""
result = spark.sql(dynamic_pivot_sql)
*/

-- 4. UNPIVOT: Wide → Long format
SELECT account_id, metric_name, metric_value
FROM (
    SELECT
        account_id,
        balance_current,
        balance_savings,
        balance_loan,
        credit_limit
    FROM gold_account_balances
    WHERE snapshot_date = '2024-12-31'
)
UNPIVOT (
    metric_value FOR metric_name IN (
        balance_current  AS 'CURRENT_BALANCE',
        balance_savings  AS 'SAVINGS_BALANCE',
        balance_loan     AS 'LOAN_BALANCE',
        credit_limit     AS 'CREDIT_LIMIT'
    )
)
WHERE metric_value IS NOT NULL;
notes: PIVOT requires specifying column values statically in SQL — use PySpark to generate dynamic pivot SQL for unknown categories
PIVOT with multiple aggregate functions generates N*M columns (N pivot values × M aggregations) — keep combinations manageable
UNPIVOT is essentially a structured STACK operation — equivalent to multiple UNION ALLs but more readable
Pivoted DataFrames are often used to feed Power BI or Excel-based reports via JDBC/ODBC Databricks SQL endpoints
Consider materialized gold views for pivoted reporting tables — avoids re-running expensive pivots on every report query
use_case: Building an EBA COREP capital adequacy matrix report for a European universal bank — PIVOT transforms long-format risk exposure data (one row per country-tier) into the wide-format matrix table (countries as rows, risk tiers as columns) required by the regulatory submission template.

title: Date and Timestamp Functions
description: Date and timestamp handling is critical in BFSI for interest calculations, period-end reporting, settlement date computations, and timezone normalization. Spark SQL provides a rich set of date functions fully compatible with ANSI SQL, plus Databricks-specific extensions for timezone-aware operations.
code:
-- =============================================
-- Date & Timestamp Functions
-- EU BFSI — Reporting Period & Settlement Calcs
-- =============================================

USE CATALOG eu_bfsi_prod;
USE SCHEMA silver;

SELECT
    txn_id,
    txn_timestamp,

    -- ── Current values ──────────────────────
    current_date()                          AS today,
    current_timestamp()                     AS now_utc,
    now()                                   AS now_alias,

    -- ── Extraction ──────────────────────────
    YEAR(txn_timestamp)                     AS txn_year,
    MONTH(txn_timestamp)                    AS txn_month,
    DAY(txn_timestamp)                      AS txn_day,
    DAYOFWEEK(txn_timestamp)                AS day_of_week,  -- 1=Sun
    DAYOFYEAR(txn_timestamp)                AS day_of_year,
    WEEKOFYEAR(txn_timestamp)               AS week_number,
    QUARTER(txn_timestamp)                  AS txn_quarter,
    HOUR(txn_timestamp)                     AS txn_hour,
    MINUTE(txn_timestamp)                   AS txn_minute,

    -- ── Formatting ──────────────────────────
    DATE_FORMAT(txn_timestamp, 'yyyy-MM-dd')            AS date_str,
    DATE_FORMAT(txn_timestamp, 'dd/MM/yyyy HH:mm:ss')   AS eu_datetime_str,
    DATE_FORMAT(txn_timestamp, 'MMM yyyy')              AS month_label,
    TO_DATE(txn_timestamp)                              AS date_only,

    -- ── Arithmetic ──────────────────────────
    DATE_ADD(txn_timestamp, 2)              AS value_date_t2,   -- T+2 settlement
    DATE_ADD(txn_timestamp, 30)             AS payment_due,
    DATE_SUB(txn_timestamp, 1)              AS prev_business_approx,
    ADD_MONTHS(txn_timestamp, 3)            AS quarterly_review,
    ADD_MONTHS(LAST_DAY(txn_timestamp), 1)  AS next_month_end,
    LAST_DAY(txn_timestamp)                 AS month_end,
    TRUNC(txn_timestamp, 'MM')              AS month_start,
    TRUNC(txn_timestamp, 'YEAR')            AS year_start,
    TRUNC(txn_timestamp, 'DD')              AS start_of_day,

    -- ── Differences ─────────────────────────
    DATEDIFF(current_date(), DATE(txn_timestamp))       AS days_since_txn,
    MONTHS_BETWEEN(current_date(), DATE(txn_timestamp)) AS months_since_txn,

    -- ── Timezone Conversion ──────────────────
    CONVERT_TIMEZONE('UTC', 'Europe/London', txn_timestamp)  AS ts_london,
    CONVERT_TIMEZONE('UTC', 'Europe/Paris',  txn_timestamp)  AS ts_paris,
    FROM_UTC_TIMESTAMP(txn_timestamp, 'Europe/Berlin')       AS ts_berlin,
    TO_UTC_TIMESTAMP(txn_timestamp, 'Europe/Warsaw')         AS back_to_utc,

    -- ── Unix timestamps ──────────────────────
    UNIX_TIMESTAMP(txn_timestamp)           AS epoch_seconds,
    FROM_UNIXTIME(epoch_timestamp)          AS from_epoch,
    TIMESTAMP_MILLIS(epoch_millis)          AS from_millis,

    -- ── Parsing ─────────────────────────────
    TO_TIMESTAMP('31/12/2024 23:59:59', 'dd/MM/yyyy HH:mm:ss') AS parsed_ts,
    TO_DATE('31-12-2024', 'dd-MM-yyyy')                         AS parsed_date,
    TRY_TO_TIMESTAMP('not-a-date', 'yyyy-MM-dd')                AS safe_parse  -- Returns NULL

FROM silver_transactions
WHERE txn_date = current_date() - INTERVAL 1 DAY;  -- Yesterday's transactions
notes: All Databricks timestamps are stored in UTC — always use CONVERT_TIMEZONE for European reporting (CET/CEST shift)
TRUNC(ts, 'MM') gives first day of month — essential for monthly report period boundaries
DATE_ADD operates on calendar days; business day calculations require a custom calendar table join
TRY_TO_TIMESTAMP / TRY_CAST return NULL on parse failure instead of throwing — always prefer in ETL
MONTHS_BETWEEN returns a decimal — ROUND to integer for whole-month differences in interest calculations
use_case: SEPA Direct Debit settlement date calculation engine at a European payment institution — T+2 settlement dates, CET business day reporting windows, and end-of-month position snapshots all require precise date arithmetic with timezone awareness for cross-border EUR/GBP/CHF transactions.

title: Delta Lake DML: MERGE INTO, UPDATE, DELETE
description: Delta Lake's ACID DML operations (MERGE, UPDATE, DELETE) enable true data warehouse semantics on the data lake. MERGE INTO is the most powerful — implementing upsert, delete, and conditional insert in a single atomic operation. These replace complex partition-swap workarounds previously needed with plain Parquet.
code:
-- =============================================
-- Delta Lake DML Operations
-- EU BFSI — Account & Transaction Management
-- =============================================

USE CATALOG eu_bfsi_prod;
USE SCHEMA silver;

-- ─────────────────────────────────────────────
-- 1. UPDATE — Correct account risk tiers
-- ─────────────────────────────────────────────
UPDATE silver_accounts
SET
    risk_tier           = 'HIGH',
    risk_review_date    = current_date(),
    updated_by          = current_user(),
    updated_ts          = current_timestamp()
WHERE account_id IN (
    SELECT DISTINCT account_id
    FROM silver_aml_alerts
    WHERE alert_date >= current_date() - INTERVAL 30 DAYS
      AND alert_severity = 'CRITICAL'
      AND alert_status = 'CONFIRMED'
);

-- ─────────────────────────────────────────────
-- 2. DELETE — GDPR right-to-erasure
-- ─────────────────────────────────────────────
DELETE FROM silver_customer_pii
WHERE customer_id IN (
    SELECT customer_id
    FROM gold_erasure_requests
    WHERE request_status = 'APPROVED'
      AND approved_date <= current_date()
);

-- ─────────────────────────────────────────────
-- 3. MERGE INTO — Full upsert (SCD Type 1)
-- Scenario: Intra-day account balance refresh
-- ─────────────────────────────────────────────
MERGE INTO silver_accounts AS target
USING (
    SELECT
        account_id,
        current_balance,
        available_balance,
        credit_limit,
        account_status,
        last_activity_date,
        current_timestamp() AS source_ts
    FROM bronze_account_snapshot
    WHERE snapshot_date = current_date()
      AND batch_id = '${latest_batch_id}'
) AS source
ON target.account_id = source.account_id

WHEN MATCHED AND target.account_status != source.account_status THEN
    UPDATE SET
        target.current_balance    = source.current_balance,
        target.available_balance  = source.available_balance,
        target.account_status     = source.account_status,
        target.last_activity_date = source.last_activity_date,
        target.updated_ts         = source.source_ts

WHEN MATCHED AND (
    target.current_balance   != source.current_balance  OR
    target.available_balance != source.available_balance
) THEN
    UPDATE SET
        target.current_balance    = source.current_balance,
        target.available_balance  = source.available_balance,
        target.last_activity_date = source.last_activity_date,
        target.updated_ts         = source.source_ts

WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN
    INSERT (
        account_id, current_balance, available_balance,
        credit_limit, account_status, last_activity_date,
        created_ts, updated_ts
    )
    VALUES (
        source.account_id, source.current_balance, source.available_balance,
        source.credit_limit, source.account_status, source.last_activity_date,
        source.source_ts, source.source_ts
    )

WHEN NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE AND target.account_status = 'ACTIVE' THEN
    UPDATE SET target.account_status = 'CLOSED',
               target.updated_ts = current_timestamp();
notes: MERGE INTO is atomic — all matched/not-matched clauses execute in a single transaction, never leaving partial state
WHEN NOT MATCHED BY SOURCE (Delta-specific) handles rows in target that have no match in source — enables soft-delete patterns
Multiple WHEN MATCHED clauses are evaluated in order — only the first matching clause executes per row
For large MERGE operations, add /*+ BROADCAST(source) */ hint if source is small; otherwise ensure both sides are partitioned on join key
Delta records every MERGE as a single commit — DESCRIBE HISTORY shows operationParameters with metrics
use_case: Intra-day account balance refresh at a European retail bank — MERGE INTO atomically upserts Core Banking account snapshots received every 4 hours, updating existing accounts and inserting new ones, while soft-deleting accounts no longer present in the source feed.

title: Delta Lake Time Travel: VERSION AS OF / TIMESTAMP AS OF
description: Delta Lake's time travel feature allows querying historical versions of a table using VERSION AS OF or TIMESTAMP AS OF. This enables data auditing, regulatory point-in-time reconstruction, rollback after erroneous DML, and reproducible ML training datasets from a specific snapshot in time.
code:
-- =============================================
-- Delta Time Travel
-- EU BFSI — Regulatory Point-in-Time Queries
-- =============================================

USE CATALOG eu_bfsi_prod;
USE SCHEMA silver;

-- 1. Query by version number
SELECT COUNT(*), SUM(txn_amount_eur) AS total_eur
FROM silver_transactions VERSION AS OF 142
WHERE txn_date = '2024-12-31';

-- 2. Query by timestamp (EOM snapshot for regulatory reporting)
SELECT
    account_id,
    current_balance,
    available_balance,
    account_status
FROM silver_accounts
TIMESTAMP AS OF '2024-12-31T23:59:59.000+00:00'
WHERE account_status = 'ACTIVE';

-- 3. Audit: Compare current vs past state
SELECT
    curr.account_id,
    curr.risk_tier                          AS current_risk_tier,
    hist.risk_tier                          AS risk_tier_90days_ago,
    curr.credit_limit                       AS current_limit,
    hist.credit_limit                       AS limit_90days_ago,
    curr.credit_limit - hist.credit_limit   AS limit_change
FROM silver_accounts curr
JOIN silver_accounts TIMESTAMP AS OF
    DATE_SUB(current_date(), 90) hist
    ON curr.account_id = hist.account_id
WHERE curr.risk_tier != hist.risk_tier
   OR curr.credit_limit != hist.credit_limit
ORDER BY ABS(curr.credit_limit - hist.credit_limit) DESC;

-- 4. Restore table to a previous version (ROLLBACK)
RESTORE TABLE silver_accounts
TO VERSION AS OF 98;
-- Or by timestamp:
-- RESTORE TABLE silver_accounts TO TIMESTAMP AS OF '2024-12-01 08:00:00';

-- 5. CTAS from historical snapshot
CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE eu_bfsi_prod.gold.eom_dec2024_account_snapshot
USING DELTA
COMMENT 'EOM December 2024 account snapshot for COREP reporting'
AS
SELECT *
FROM eu_bfsi_prod.silver.silver_accounts
TIMESTAMP AS OF '2024-12-31T23:59:00.000+00:00';

-- 6. Show Delta history (audit log)
DESCRIBE HISTORY silver_transactions
LIMIT 30;
-- Returns: version, timestamp, userName, operation, operationParameters, operationMetrics

-- 7. Find version closest to a business event timestamp
SELECT version, timestamp, operation, operationMetrics
FROM (
    DESCRIBE HISTORY eu_bfsi_prod.silver.silver_transactions
)
WHERE timestamp <= '2024-12-31T18:00:00.000+00:00'
ORDER BY timestamp DESC
LIMIT 1;
notes: Time travel is only available within the retention window — default 30 days, configurable via delta.deletedFileRetentionDuration
RESTORE TABLE is atomic — it adds a new commit pointing to historical files, rather than replaying old operations
VERSION AS OF is cheaper than TIMESTAMP AS OF — the version→file mapping is O(1) while timestamp requires log scanning
Historical snapshots are available even after OPTIMIZE/VACUUM — but VACUUM with retentionHours=0 deletes old files immediately
Use DESCRIBE HISTORY to find exact version numbers before using VERSION AS OF in audits
use_case: A European bank's regulatory team reconstructing a point-in-time account position snapshot for an ECB audit — TIMESTAMP AS OF '2024-12-31T23:59:59' retrieves the exact end-of-year state used for COREP capital adequacy reporting, without any manual archiving.

title: LATERAL VIEW and Subqueries (Scalar, Correlated)
description: LATERAL VIEW is used to explode complex types (arrays, maps) into virtual columns while keeping the original row context. Scalar and correlated subqueries allow embedding per-row calculations and existence checks that reference the outer query. These are powerful for complex enrichment patterns in financial data pipelines.
code:
-- =============================================
-- LATERAL VIEW & Subqueries
-- EU BFSI — Trade & Account Enrichment
-- =============================================

USE CATALOG eu_bfsi_prod;
USE SCHEMA silver;

-- 1. LATERAL VIEW EXPLODE with alias
SELECT
    t.trade_id,
    t.trade_date,
    t.counterparty_id,
    leg.leg_type,
    leg.notional,
    leg.currency,
    leg.start_date,
    leg.end_date
FROM silver_trades t
LATERAL VIEW EXPLODE(t.trade_legs) AS leg
WHERE leg.currency = 'EUR'
  AND leg.notional > 10000000;

-- 2. Multiple LATERAL VIEW (cross-product of arrays)
SELECT
    account_id,
    flag_type,
    flag_value,
    product_code
FROM silver_accounts
LATERAL VIEW EXPLODE(risk_flags)    AS flag_type
LATERAL VIEW EXPLODE(product_codes) AS product_code
WHERE flag_type IN ('AML_ALERT', 'SANCTIONS_MATCH');

-- 3. LATERAL VIEW OUTER (keeps rows even if array is empty/null)
SELECT
    c.customer_id,
    c.customer_name,
    acc.account_id
FROM silver_customers c
LATERAL VIEW OUTER EXPLODE(c.linked_account_ids) AS account_id;

-- 4. Scalar subquery — single value per row
SELECT
    t.txn_id,
    t.account_id,
    t.txn_amount,
    -- Scalar subquery: account's monthly average for comparison
    (
        SELECT ROUND(AVG(txn_amount), 2)
        FROM silver_transactions inner_t
        WHERE inner_t.account_id = t.account_id
          AND YEAR(inner_t.txn_date)  = YEAR(t.txn_date)
          AND MONTH(inner_t.txn_date) = MONTH(t.txn_date)
          AND inner_t.txn_id != t.txn_id
    )                                       AS monthly_avg_excl_self,
    t.txn_amount - (
        SELECT ROUND(AVG(txn_amount), 2)
        FROM silver_transactions inner_t
        WHERE inner_t.account_id = t.account_id
    )                                       AS deviation_from_lifetime_avg
FROM silver_transactions t
WHERE t.txn_date = current_date() - INTERVAL 1 DAY
  AND t.txn_type = 'DEBIT'
  AND t.txn_amount > 50000;

-- 5. Correlated EXISTS subquery — AML alert filter
SELECT a.account_id, a.customer_id, a.risk_tier
FROM silver_accounts a
WHERE EXISTS (
    SELECT 1
    FROM silver_transactions t
    WHERE t.account_id = a.account_id
      AND t.txn_amount > 500000
      AND t.txn_date >= current_date() - INTERVAL 7 DAYS
      AND t.counterparty_country NOT IN ('DE','FR','NL','BE','ES','IT')
);

-- 6. NOT EXISTS — accounts with no transactions in 12 months (dormant)
SELECT a.account_id, a.customer_id, a.account_type
FROM silver_accounts a
WHERE a.account_status = 'ACTIVE'
  AND NOT EXISTS (
    SELECT 1
    FROM silver_transactions t
    WHERE t.account_id = a.account_id
      AND t.txn_date >= current_date() - INTERVAL 365 DAYS
  );
notes: LATERAL VIEW OUTER preserves rows where the array/map is NULL or empty — critical for outer join semantics with explode
Correlated scalar subqueries execute once per row — replace with window functions for large datasets to avoid N+1 execution
EXISTS is more efficient than IN with subquery — Spark converts EXISTS to a semi-join internally
Multiple LATERAL VIEW clauses produce a cartesian product of the arrays — ensure this is the intended behavior
Spark 3.x can optimize correlated subqueries through decorrelation — EXPLAIN EXTENDED reveals if optimization fired
use_case: AML screening at a European bank — correlated EXISTS subquery identifies accounts with recent large cross-border transactions to non-EU countries, while LATERAL VIEW EXPLODE processes multi-leg structured product trades from the derivatives portfolio system.

title: MERGE INTO for SCD Type 2 (Slowly Changing Dimensions)
description: SCD Type 2 preserves full history by closing old records and inserting new versions when dimension attributes change. Delta's MERGE INTO with multiple WHEN clauses implements SCD2 atomically. This pattern is critical for financial systems where account and customer attribute history must be preserved for regulatory audit trails.
code:
-- =============================================
-- SCD Type 2 with MERGE INTO
-- EU BFSI — Customer Risk Profile History
-- =============================================

USE CATALOG eu_bfsi_prod;
USE SCHEMA silver;

-- Target SCD2 table structure:
-- CREATE TABLE silver_dim_customer (
--     surrogate_key   BIGINT GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY,
--     customer_id     STRING NOT NULL,
--     customer_name   STRING,
--     risk_tier       STRING,
--     kyc_status      STRING,
--     pep_flag        BOOLEAN,
--     nationality     STRING,
--     effective_from  TIMESTAMP NOT NULL,
--     effective_to    TIMESTAMP,  -- NULL = current active record
--     is_current      BOOLEAN NOT NULL,
--     record_hash     STRING NOT NULL,  -- MD5 of SCD2 attributes
--     created_ts      TIMESTAMP,
--     updated_ts      TIMESTAMP
-- ) USING DELTA
-- TBLPROPERTIES ('delta.enableChangeDataFeed' = 'true');

-- Stage incoming changes with hash for change detection
CREATE OR REPLACE TEMPORARY VIEW v_customer_changes AS
SELECT
    customer_id,
    customer_name,
    risk_tier,
    kyc_status,
    pep_flag,
    nationality,
    current_timestamp()                                         AS effective_from,
    MD5(CONCAT_WS('|',
        COALESCE(risk_tier, ''),
        COALESCE(kyc_status, ''),
        COALESCE(CAST(pep_flag AS STRING), ''),
        COALESCE(nationality, '')
    ))                                                          AS record_hash
FROM bronze_customer_updates
WHERE batch_date = current_date();

-- Step 1: Close existing active records that have changed
MERGE INTO silver_dim_customer AS target
USING (
    SELECT
        src.customer_id,
        src.record_hash                 AS new_hash,
        tgt.surrogate_key               AS old_surrogate_key
    FROM v_customer_changes src
    JOIN silver_dim_customer tgt
        ON  src.customer_id = tgt.customer_id
        AND tgt.is_current = true
        AND src.record_hash != tgt.record_hash  -- Attribute change detected
) AS changed_records
ON target.surrogate_key = changed_records.old_surrogate_key
WHEN MATCHED THEN
    UPDATE SET
        target.effective_to = current_timestamp() - INTERVAL 1 MILLISECOND,
        target.is_current   = false,
        target.updated_ts   = current_timestamp();

-- Step 2: Insert new versions for changed records + new customers
MERGE INTO silver_dim_customer AS target
USING (
    -- New versions for changed existing records
    SELECT
        src.customer_id,
        src.customer_name,
        src.risk_tier,
        src.kyc_status,
        src.pep_flag,
        src.nationality,
        src.effective_from,
        NULL                AS effective_to,
        true                AS is_current,
        src.record_hash,
        current_timestamp() AS created_ts,
        current_timestamp() AS updated_ts
    FROM v_customer_changes src
    -- Rows that had existing records but changed
    WHERE EXISTS (
        SELECT 1 FROM silver_dim_customer tgt
        WHERE tgt.customer_id = src.customer_id
          AND tgt.is_current = false
          AND tgt.updated_ts >= current_timestamp() - INTERVAL 5 MINUTES
    )
    UNION ALL
    -- Entirely new customers
    SELECT
        src.customer_id,
        src.customer_name,
        src.risk_tier,
        src.kyc_status,
        src.pep_flag,
        src.nationality,
        src.effective_from,
        NULL                AS effective_to,
        true                AS is_current,
        src.record_hash,
        current_timestamp() AS created_ts,
        current_timestamp() AS updated_ts
    FROM v_customer_changes src
    WHERE NOT EXISTS (
        SELECT 1 FROM silver_dim_customer tgt
        WHERE tgt.customer_id = src.customer_id
    )
) AS new_records
ON 1 = 0  -- Never match — always INSERT
WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN
    INSERT (
        customer_id, customer_name, risk_tier, kyc_status,
        pep_flag, nationality, effective_from, effective_to,
        is_current, record_hash, created_ts, updated_ts
    )
    VALUES (
        new_records.customer_id, new_records.customer_name,
        new_records.risk_tier, new_records.kyc_status,
        new_records.pep_flag, new_records.nationality,
        new_records.effective_from, new_records.effective_to,
        new_records.is_current, new_records.record_hash,
        new_records.created_ts, new_records.updated_ts
    );
notes: Two-step MERGE is required for SCD2: Step 1 closes old records, Step 2 inserts new versions — keeps logic clear
MD5/SHA hash on SCD2 attributes enables efficient change detection without comparing every column individually
ON 1 = 0 is the 'insert-only MERGE' pattern — forces all rows to go to the WHEN NOT MATCHED branch
is_current flag + NULL effective_to identifies current records; always index/cluster on (customer_id, is_current)
Consider GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY for surrogate keys — Delta natively supports identity columns since DBR 10.4
use_case: Customer risk profile history at a European private bank — SCD2 preserves complete audit trail of risk tier changes required by MiFID II suitability assessments, allowing retrospective analysis of whether a customer was classified correctly at the time of each investment recommendation.

title: OPTIMIZE and Z-ORDER BY for Delta Performance
description: OPTIMIZE compacts small Delta files into optimal-sized Parquet files (typically 1GB target), dramatically improving query scan performance. Z-ORDER BY co-locates data with similar values of specified columns within files, enabling data skipping. Together they are the primary performance tuning levers for Delta tables in Databricks.
code:
-- =============================================
-- OPTIMIZE & Z-ORDER — Delta Table Tuning
-- EU BFSI — Transaction Table Optimization
-- =============================================

USE CATALOG eu_bfsi_prod;
USE SCHEMA silver;

-- 1. Basic OPTIMIZE — compact small files
OPTIMIZE silver_transactions;

-- 2. OPTIMIZE with Z-ORDER (co-locate data by query columns)
OPTIMIZE silver_transactions
ZORDER BY (account_id, txn_currency, txn_date);
-- Tip: Z-ORDER on columns most used in WHERE/JOIN predicates

-- 3. OPTIMIZE a specific partition (incremental — new data only)
OPTIMIZE silver_transactions
WHERE txn_date = current_date() - INTERVAL 1 DAY
ZORDER BY (account_id, txn_currency);

-- 4. Check optimization statistics
DESCRIBE DETAIL silver_transactions;
-- Shows: numFiles, sizeInBytes, numPartitions, minReaderVersion

-- 5. ANALYZE TABLE — compute statistics for the query optimizer
ANALYZE TABLE silver_transactions COMPUTE STATISTICS;
ANALYZE TABLE silver_transactions COMPUTE STATISTICS FOR COLUMNS
    account_id, txn_currency, txn_amount, txn_date;

-- 6. Set auto-optimize properties
ALTER TABLE silver_transactions
SET TBLPROPERTIES (
    'delta.autoOptimize.optimizeWrite'  = 'true',  -- Compact on write
    'delta.autoOptimize.autoCompact'    = 'true',  -- Background compaction
    'delta.targetFileSize'              = '134217728',  -- 128MB target
    'delta.tuneFileSizesForRewrites'    = 'true'   -- Optimize for MERGE
);

-- 7. VACUUM — remove old/deleted files (safe to run after OPTIMIZE)
-- Default retention = 7 days. Never set to 0 in production.
VACUUM silver_transactions RETAIN 168 HOURS;  -- 7 days
-- Dry run first:
VACUUM silver_transactions DRY RUN;           -- Shows files to be deleted

-- 8. Liquid Clustering (DBR 13.3+) — dynamic, incremental clustering
-- Applied at CREATE time:
-- CREATE TABLE ... CLUSTER BY (account_id, txn_currency);

-- Add/change cluster keys on existing table:
ALTER TABLE silver_transactions
CLUSTER BY (account_id, txn_currency, txn_date);

-- Run clustering (equivalent to OPTIMIZE for liquid clustering)
OPTIMIZE silver_transactions;
-- Databricks auto-selects Z-ORDER columns from CLUSTER BY definition

-- 9. Bloom filter index for equality predicates
CREATE BLOOMFILTER INDEX ON TABLE silver_transactions
FOR COLUMNS (txn_id OPTIONS (fpp=0.01, numItems=1000000000));
-- fpp = false positive probability; lower = larger index but better filtering
notes: ZORDER BY significantly improves data skipping — Delta skips entire files when min/max column statistics don't overlap the query predicate
Z-ORDER is most effective on high-cardinality columns used in WHERE clauses; avoid low-cardinality columns (e.g., boolean flags)
Liquid Clustering is the modern replacement for both static partitioning and Z-ORDER — supports incremental re-clustering without full rewrites
VACUUM permanently deletes files — ensure no active time travel queries or streaming checkpoints reference older versions before running
OPTIMIZE is idempotent — run it in production pipelines after bulk loads; use WHERE clause to target only new partitions
use_case: Post-load optimization for a European bank's silver transaction table receiving 50M+ daily records — OPTIMIZE with Z-ORDER on (account_id, txn_currency) reduces AML query scan time from 4 minutes to 18 seconds by enabling Delta data skipping to eliminate 94% of files for account-specific queries.

title: Delta Change Data Feed (CDF) — SQL
description: Delta Change Data Feed (CDF) captures row-level change events (insert, update_preimage, update_postimage, delete) on Delta tables. It enables efficient incremental propagation through Medallion layers, CDC pipelines, and audit logging without full table scans. CDF is enabled per table and queryable via SQL.
code:
-- =============================================
-- Delta Change Data Feed (CDF)
-- EU BFSI — Incremental Silver→Gold Propagation
-- =============================================

USE CATALOG eu_bfsi_prod;
USE SCHEMA silver;

-- 1. Enable CDF on existing table
ALTER TABLE silver_accounts
SET TBLPROPERTIES ('delta.enableChangeDataFeed' = 'true');

-- 2. Read changes since a specific version
SELECT
    _change_type,       -- insert | update_preimage | update_postimage | delete
    _commit_version,    -- Delta version of the commit
    _commit_timestamp,  -- Timestamp of the commit
    account_id,
    risk_tier,
    kyc_status,
    account_status
FROM table_changes('eu_bfsi_prod.silver.silver_accounts', 150)
ORDER BY _commit_version, _change_type;

-- 3. Read changes between version range
SELECT *
FROM table_changes('eu_bfsi_prod.silver.silver_accounts', 100, 200);

-- 4. Read changes since a timestamp
SELECT *
FROM table_changes(
    'eu_bfsi_prod.silver.silver_accounts',
    '2024-12-01T00:00:00.000+00:00'
);

-- 5. Practical: Only get UPDATES (before/after pair)
SELECT
    pre.account_id,
    pre.risk_tier         AS old_risk_tier,
    post.risk_tier        AS new_risk_tier,
    pre.kyc_status        AS old_kyc_status,
    post.kyc_status       AS new_kyc_status,
    post._commit_timestamp AS change_ts
FROM table_changes('eu_bfsi_prod.silver.silver_accounts',
                   '2024-12-01T00:00:00.000+00:00') pre
JOIN table_changes('eu_bfsi_prod.silver.silver_accounts',
                   '2024-12-01T00:00:00.000+00:00') post
    ON pre.account_id = post.account_id
    AND pre._commit_version  = post._commit_version
    AND pre._change_type  = 'update_preimage'
    AND post._change_type = 'update_postimage'
WHERE pre.risk_tier != post.risk_tier;  -- Only risk tier changes

-- 6. CDF for incremental gold layer propagation
INSERT INTO eu_bfsi_prod.gold.gold_account_risk_changes
SELECT
    account_id,
    _change_type            AS change_type,
    _commit_version         AS source_version,
    _commit_timestamp       AS change_ts,
    risk_tier,
    kyc_status,
    current_timestamp()     AS processed_ts
FROM table_changes(
    'eu_bfsi_prod.silver.silver_accounts',
    (
        SELECT COALESCE(MAX(source_version), 0)
        FROM eu_bfsi_prod.gold.gold_account_risk_changes
    )  -- Start from last processed version
)
WHERE _change_type IN ('update_postimage', 'insert');
notes: CDF captures update_preimage (before) and update_postimage (after) for each UPDATE — join them on account_id + _commit_version for before/after comparison
CDF storage overhead is minimal — it stores only the changed rows, not full snapshots
Use _commit_version watermarking pattern (MAX of last processed version) for idempotent incremental loads
CDF works with streaming: spark.readStream.format('delta').option('readChangeFeed', 'true').load(path)
CDF requires minReaderVersion=2 and minWriterVersion=4 — automatically set when enabling CDF
use_case: Incremental silver→gold propagation at a European asset management firm — CDF eliminates the need to full-scan the 2-billion-row silver_accounts table nightly; instead the gold layer processes only the ~50,000 daily changed rows, reducing pipeline runtime from 2 hours to 3 minutes.

title: Streaming Queries in Spark SQL
description: Spark Structured Streaming exposes a SQL interface for building real-time pipelines. In Databricks, streaming SQL queries can read from Delta tables, Kafka, or Event Hubs as sources and write to Delta as sinks. Trigger options control micro-batch frequency, enabling near-real-time fraud detection and payment processing.
code:
-- =============================================
-- Structured Streaming in Spark SQL
-- EU BFSI — Real-time Payment Fraud Detection
-- =============================================

-- Note: Full streaming setup done via PySpark API;
-- SQL cells in Databricks can run streaming queries
-- using CREATE STREAMING TABLE (DLT) or via SQL API.

-- ── In Databricks SQL (non-DLT) ─────────────────
-- Use spark.sql() from PySpark notebook:

-- PySpark bootstrap for streaming:
-- stream_df = (
--   spark.readStream
--     .format('delta')
--     .option('readChangeFeed', 'true')
--     .option('startingVersion', 'latest')
--     .table('eu_bfsi_prod.bronze.bronze_transactions')
-- )
-- stream_df.createOrReplaceTempView('streaming_transactions')

-- ── Then query with SQL ──────────────────────────

-- 1. Streaming aggregation with watermark (SQL via spark.sql)
-- SELECT
--     window(txn_timestamp, '5 minutes').start  AS window_start,
--     window(txn_timestamp, '5 minutes').end    AS window_end,
--     account_id,
--     COUNT(*)                                  AS txn_count_5min,
--     SUM(txn_amount)                           AS volume_5min,
--     MAX(txn_amount)                           AS max_txn_5min
-- FROM streaming_transactions
-- GROUP BY window(txn_timestamp, '5 minutes'), account_id

-- ── Full PySpark Streaming Example ──────────────
/*
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

# Read stream from Delta CDF
stream = (
    spark.readStream
        .format('delta')
        .option('readChangeFeed', 'true')
        .option('startingTimestamp', '2024-01-01')
        .table('eu_bfsi_prod.bronze.bronze_transactions')
        .where("_change_type = 'insert'")
)

# Apply fraud detection aggregation
fraud_alerts = (
    stream
    .withWatermark('txn_timestamp', '10 minutes')
    .groupBy(
        F.window('txn_timestamp', '5 minutes'),
        'account_id'
    )
    .agg(
        F.count('*').alias('txn_count'),
        F.sum('txn_amount').alias('total_amount'),
        F.collect_set('counterparty_country').alias('countries')
    )
    .where('txn_count > 10 OR total_amount > 100000')
)

# Write to Delta alert table
query = (
    fraud_alerts.writeStream
        .format('delta')
        .outputMode('append')
        .option('checkpointLocation',
                'abfss://checkpoints@euadlsprod.dfs.core.windows.net/fraud_stream/')
        .trigger(processingTime='30 seconds')
        .toTable('eu_bfsi_prod.gold.gold_realtime_fraud_alerts')
)
*/

-- ── Foreground streaming Delta table query ───────
-- After streaming writes, query the output table normally:
SELECT
    window_start,
    window_end,
    account_id,
    txn_count_5min,
    volume_5min,
    SIZE(countries)         AS unique_countries,
    CASE
        WHEN txn_count_5min > 50  THEN 'HIGH_VELOCITY'
        WHEN volume_5min > 500000 THEN 'HIGH_VALUE'
        ELSE 'STANDARD'
    END                     AS alert_type,
    current_timestamp()     AS alerted_ts
FROM eu_bfsi_prod.gold.gold_realtime_fraud_alerts
WHERE window_start >= current_timestamp() - INTERVAL 1 HOUR
ORDER BY volume_5min DESC;
notes: Watermarks define how late data is tolerated before a streaming window closes — critical for out-of-order payment events
Trigger(processingTime='30 seconds') creates micro-batches; Trigger(once=True) processes all available data once (batch-streaming hybrid)
Checkpoints store streaming state — always use ADLS Gen2 paths for fault-tolerant, resumable streams in Azure Databricks
Delta's exactly-once semantics with idempotent writes ensure no duplicate alerts even after stream failures and restarts
Use Delta Live Tables (DLT) for production streaming — it manages checkpoints, restarts, and monitoring automatically
use_case: Real-time payment fraud detection at a European payments processor — 5-minute tumbling windows on transaction streams detect velocity attacks (>10 transactions in 5 minutes) and high-value anomalies, triggering fraud alerts to Visa/Mastercard within 30 seconds of suspicious activity.

title: Schema Enforcement and Schema Evolution in Delta
description: Delta Lake enforces schema on write by default, rejecting data that doesn't match the table schema. Schema evolution allows controlled schema changes (adding columns, widening types) via configuration or DDL. Understanding when to enforce vs evolve schemas is critical for data quality and pipeline reliability in BFSI environments.
code:
-- =============================================
-- Schema Enforcement & Evolution
-- EU BFSI — Handling Source Schema Changes
-- =============================================

USE CATALOG eu_bfsi_prod;
USE SCHEMA silver;

-- 1. Schema enforcement is ON by default
-- This INSERT will FAIL if source has extra/missing columns:
-- INSERT INTO silver_transactions SELECT * FROM bronze_with_new_cols;
-- Error: A schema mismatch detected when writing to the Delta table

-- 2. Enable schema evolution for MERGE/INSERT
-- Option A: Session-level config
SET spark.databricks.delta.schema.autoMerge.enabled = true;

-- 3. Add columns via ALTER TABLE (preferred explicit approach)
ALTER TABLE silver_transactions
    ADD COLUMN iban_sender  STRING COMMENT 'IBAN of sending account (SEPA mandate)',
    ADD COLUMN iban_receiver STRING COMMENT 'IBAN of receiving account (SEPA mandate)',
    ADD COLUMN sepa_mandate_ref STRING COMMENT 'SEPA direct debit mandate reference';

-- 4. Rename column (requires columnMapping mode = name)
ALTER TABLE silver_transactions
    RENAME COLUMN txn_status TO transaction_status;

-- 5. Drop column (soft-drop with column mapping)
ALTER TABLE silver_transactions
    DROP COLUMN legacy_batch_code;
-- Note: Data is NOT physically removed — column mapping hides it
-- Physical removal requires REORG TABLE ... APPLY (PURGE)

REORG TABLE silver_transactions APPLY (PURGE);
-- This rewrites Parquet files without dropped columns

-- 6. Change column comment
ALTER TABLE silver_transactions
    ALTER COLUMN txn_amount
    COMMENT 'Transaction amount in originating currency — DECIMAL(18,4)';

-- 7. Column mapping modes
ALTER TABLE silver_transactions
SET TBLPROPERTIES (
    'delta.columnMapping.mode' = 'name',  -- Enables rename/drop
    'delta.minReaderVersion'   = '2',
    'delta.minWriterVersion'   = '5'
);

-- 8. Schema evolution in MERGE (with autoMerge enabled)
